title: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law
author: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: McCormack advances the contrary, largely predictive view that AI-enabled dispute resolution can make legal processes more accessible and fair, reduce institutional burdens and extend effective justice to previously excluded users. Her responsible-implementation caveat does not alter that direction, although the supplied evidence does not establish population-level outcomes.
qs: By automating these labor-intensive tasks, AI is making                            mediation and arbitration more efficient, accessible and fair.
Done responsibly, AI can transform dispute resolution from an expensive boutique service   into an inclusive public utility, strengthening trust in both legal institutions and the rule of   law.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source does not establish the cluster’s buyer-side claim that legal departments will capture AI gains or exert pricing pressure. Instead, it redirects attention toward practical adoption within the profession, unequal access to secure tools and specialist talent, and uncertain downstream risks, while still aligning with the cluster’s emphasis on organisational capacity and workforce consequences.
qs: The cost of obtaining or training staff to assist the lawyers to exploit fully the capabilities of the tools is higher than expected.
We do not yet know all of the problems that                      might arise from the use of generative AI.

st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: The source does not assess the cluster’s empirical concern that cheaper AI-assisted filings may increase self-representation and shift screening costs without proven outcome gains. Instead, it frames generative AI prospectively as a means to improve assistance and court administration, while calling for safeguards against misuse. Its claims are predictions and programming evidence, not demonstrated justice outcomes.
qs: These efforts to advance access to justice                      will range from how to provide better and more efficient advocacy, to                      helping self-represented litigants navigate an increasingly complicated                      legal system, simplifying legal processes, preventing legal disputes, and                      avoiding the need to invoke formal legal decision-making systems.
Corresponding efforts will be needed to avoid mischief in  the application of GAI, and to ensure technology does not undercut efforts to enhance  access to justice.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s account that current legal AI remains concentrated in routine tasks while agentic task-chaining is emerging. It materially extends the operating-model thesis by identifying secure-tool costs, technological stratification and scarce implementation expertise as practical constraints beyond licence acquisition.
qs: But as the platforms become more sophisticated and begin to chain together tasks – whether called robotic process automation or agentic AI – lawyers’ creativity in exploring the bounds of AI tools presents interesting challenges for the legal profession and for the innovation teams supporting them.
The cost of obtaining or training staff to assist the lawyers to exploit fully the capabilities of the tools is higher than expected.

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: The report accepts the need to combine practical AI competence with critical thinking, ethics and human-centered professional preparation. It materially extends that position through concrete curricular examples, simulations and continuous-updating recommendations, while offering descriptive evidence rather than measured durable-learning outcomes.
qs: The program      offers hands-on experience with legal AI tools such as Spellbook and CoCounsel, educates      on the AI regulatory landscape, and advises on ethical considerations with AI in law      practice.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s concern that hallucinations make verification a potentially significant cost, while treating net utility as an empirical question rather than a settled negative conclusion. It materially develops the cluster by proposing context-sensitive, real-world evaluation that measures how risks, usage and procedures affect practical utility in deployment.
qs: The propensity of hallucinations in AI-generated content creates questions for legal professionals, chief among them - “if I have to go through my entire legal brief and fact check what the AI tool generated, is it actually creating any value or utility?”.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core proposition that existing professional duties must govern legal AI through active human oversight, verification and institutional risk management. It materially develops that position by identifying an implementation gap—quality standards must be adopted by developers to be effective—and by assigning continuing coordination and shared-resource functions to the ABA Center for Innovation. Its forecasts and access-to-justice use cases are presented as potential rather than established outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.
qs: While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

That challenge   – achieving actual adoption of good assessment standards – has generated little discussion   to date and needs attention now to ensure prudent implementation of AI to address   inequities in access to justice.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts responsible, risk-aware AI integration and materially strengthens the cluster’s implementation focus with survey evidence that many attorneys lack the familiarity and confidence needed to navigate automated systems. Its multidisciplinary guide further aligns with practical adoption attentive to confidentiality, accuracy, bias, privacy and security, although it does not demonstrate service outcomes.
qs: Of key survey findings, while most attorneys are aware that automated systems affect their clients, many are unfamiliar with how these systems work and lack confidence in explaining or navigating them.
While AI can drastically boost efficiency, it simultaneously comes   with threats to client confidentiality, potentially inaccurate or biased outputs,   privacy and security issues, and more.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational capability rather than software access alone, and materially extends the cluster by identifying secure infrastructure, professional licensing and scarce implementation expertise as additional costs that may stratify firms into technology “haves” and “have-nots.” Its contribution is qualitative and predictive, not evidence of realised market-wide returns.
qs: Predictably, the legal industry is moving toward a stratification of firms into various degrees of technology “haves” and “have-nots.” While consumer-grade AI tools are becoming increasingly sophisticated, they present privacy and confidentiality risks.
The cost of obtaining or training staff to assist the lawyers to exploit fully the capabilities of the tools is higher than expected.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core copilot proposition—selective automation with continuing human oversight—and materially develops it through concrete lifecycle governance, real-world evaluation, training, organisational-change and access-to-justice measures. It also reinforces the cluster’s cautions about verification costs, uneven access and uncertain downstream effects.
qs: AI should augment instead of replace human oversight in legal practice.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The source supports conditional judicial AI assistance subject to human verification, retained judicial responsibility, confidentiality safeguards and procedural fairness. It directly reinforces the cluster’s distinction between assistance and delegation, while treating disclosure as dependent on local rules rather than endorsing a uniform regime.
qs: Although AI and GenAI can serve as valuable aids in performing certain judicial functions, judges remain solely responsible for their decisions and must maintain proficiency in understanding and appropriately using these tools.
While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

st.t: AI governance: Literacy and benchmarking build capacity
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s framing of AI adoption as a governance and capacity-building challenge. It centres lawyer-led policies, risk frameworks, education, human oversight, verification and confidentiality safeguards, while distinguishing judicial assistance from governance of AI-generated evidence. Its access-to-justice and productivity claims are appropriately presented mainly as demonstrations or expectations rather than measured outcomes.
qs: They outline how attorneys are defining AI policies, overseeing risk frameworks, and guiding clients through responsible AI adoption.
models and verifying AI-generated content—and encourages transparency with clients about  AI use.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The report supports the synthesis’s account of expanding, multifaceted AI education through compulsory instruction, hands-on tool use, ethics, governance and simulations. Its survey and programme examples document adoption and intended learning opportunities, but provide no comparative evidence on educational effectiveness or a clear position on when restrictions versus exposure should begin.
qs: The results showed that 55% of the 29 respondent law schools offered classes on AI, and 83% reported availability of opportunities like clinics where students can learn how to use AI tools hands-on.

The program      offers hands-on experience with legal AI tools such as Spellbook and CoCounsel, educates      on the AI regulatory landscape, and advises on ethical considerations with AI in law      practice.

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s core proposition by treating insurance as one component of broader lifecycle governance, not a substitute for legal compliance or risk controls. It also reinforces that actual protection depends on careful scrutiny of exclusions, restrictions and tailored policy wording, while making no strong claims about loss prevalence or pricing.
qs: AI governance is essential for managing the unique challenges posed by artificial intelligence, which requires approaches extending beyond traditional compliance frameworks.

Businesses purchasing these novel insurance products should scrutinize their wordings carefully, with the help of counsel if necessary, to make sure that they unambiguously provide the scope of coverage promised and expected.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s assistive, human-accountable model: judges retain sole decision-making responsibility, all AI outputs require human verification, and judicial applications remain conditional on safeguards for bias, confidentiality and consequential uses. Its provisional guidelines and call for regular revision also align with the cluster’s emphasis on evolving governance rather than proven operational effectiveness.
qs: Although AI and GenAI can serve as valuable aids in performing certain judicial functions, judges remain solely responsible for their decisions and must maintain proficiency in understanding and appropriately using these tools.
While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The report directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: AI may assist judicial and dispute-resolution work, but human decision-makers retain authority and responsibility, must verify outputs, and must apply confidentiality, security and evolving governance safeguards. It offers practical guidance rather than quantitative evidence of outcomes.
qs: Although AI and GenAI can serve as valuable aids in performing certain judicial functions, judges remain solely responsible for their decisions and must maintain proficiency in understanding and appropriately using these tools.
While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition that beneficial AI adoption should be paired with enforceable, risk-based safeguards and continuing organizational accountability. It also reinforces that existing law already applies to AI, while standards and certification provide emerging governance infrastructure rather than proof of effectiveness. It offers limited evidence on EU simplification delays or cross-border convergence.
qs: Legal Precedents and Current Regulatory Landscape The panelists emphasized that AI is not operating in a regulatory vacuum.

st.t: Federal procurement: Acquisition speed can weaken accountability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that accelerated federal AI adoption must be coupled with accountability safeguards and continuing evaluation. It reports pressure to remove procurement barriers while emphasizing mandatory pre-deployment testing, impact assessment, ongoing monitoring and human oversight; it also identifies undefined procurement-neutrality criteria as an accountability limitation. It does not materially develop the cluster’s detailed claims about contractual protections, vendor evidence, lifecycle costs or lock-in.
qs: Federal agencies are encouraged to expand their use of AI tools, and under Pillar I the Plan requires that they identify and eliminate regulatory and procurement barriers to AI innovation.

st.t: Firm adoption: Access outruns dependable integration
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core distinction between growing AI uptake and dependable firm-wide integration. It says adoption remains concentrated in manageable, routine tasks while secure infrastructure, professional licences and scarce implementation expertise impose substantial additional costs; it also anticipates technology-based stratification among firms. Its evidence is qualitative and does not establish firm-wide productivity or financial returns.
qs: Outlook on AI Adoption Early adoption has been limited largely to low-risk, routine tasks where the benefits are clear and the risks are manageable.
The adoption of AI tools inevitably means there are also related costs that firms are just beginning to experience over and above licensing.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The report directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: AI may assist legal and judicial work, but humans retain authority and responsibility, and all outputs require verification. It also aligns with bounded, task-sensitive adoption, confidentiality safeguards and evolving organisational governance, while offering little quantitative evidence on model reliability or sanctions patterns.
qs: Although AI and GenAI can serve as valuable aids in performing certain judicial functions, judges remain solely responsible for their decisions and must maintain proficiency in understanding and appropriately using these tools.
While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The report documents substantial curricular exposure and hands-on AI activity but does not present these as evidence of durable competence. Its explicit concern that AI reliance may erode junior lawyers’ core skills reinforces the cluster’s distinction between adoption and professional readiness, though the concern remains unresolved rather than empirically established.
qs: The results showed that 55% of the 29 respondent law schools offered classes on AI, and 83% reported availability of opportunities like clinics where students can learn how to use AI tools hands-on.
Will reliance on GenAI                      erode junior associates’ drafting and research skills, resulting in a   generation of new lawyers who are simply worse at their jobs?

st.t: Judicial integrity: Controlled assistance replaces blanket bans
st.an: The source supports controlled judicial use by offering a responsible-use framework rather than advocating prohibition, and it aligns AI governance with judicial ethics and institutional integrity. Its general, non-final guidance does not materially extend the cluster’s operational safeguards or provide empirical evidence.
qs: They provide a framework for how you can use AI and generative AI             responsibly as judicial officers.
These Guidelines are neither intended to be exhaustive nor the final word on this subject.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s balance: AI can expand provider capacity and direct public assistance, but public-facing use requires rigorous quality evaluation, affordability, human verification and safeguards against misinformation and unequal access. Its evidence is mainly programmatic and prospective rather than proof of improved population-level legal outcomes.
qs: It described the potential for generative AI to improve access to justice in two ways:  1.by increasing the efficiency and productivity of legal services and pro bono lawyers, so that    they can assist many more people with higher levels of service; and  2.by making accurate, usable, and understandable legal information and assistance easily    available to individuals with civil legal problems.

Rigorous evaluation of AI tools that individuals without lawyers might use for assistance with their civil problems is important to protect the public from inaccurate and potentially harmful information and to facilitate the development of accurate and useful tools.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious proposition that AI may weaken junior skill development and impose substantial verification burdens, while treating these as unresolved risks rather than demonstrated profession-wide effects. It also reinforces the cluster’s view that adoption is costly and operationally demanding, but does not directly establish changes to leverage, associate revenue or the law-firm pyramid.
qs: Will reliance on GenAI                      erode junior associates’ drafting and research skills, resulting in a   generation of new lawyers who are simply worse at their jobs?

Will we end up with a   briefing process that is less efficient, not more, and thus more expensive, because we will   have to work harder to tell fact from fiction when responding to briefs that were created   using GenAI?

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the proposition that generative AI could expand legal assistance and help self-represented litigants, while acknowledging that misuse could undermine access to justice. Its claims are predominantly prospective and do not resolve the cluster’s questions about protection boundaries, accountability, or measured outcomes.
qs: These efforts to advance access to justice                      will range from how to provide better and more efficient advocacy, to                      helping self-represented litigants navigate an increasingly complicated                      legal system, simplifying legal processes, preventing legal disputes, and                      avoiding the need to invoke formal legal decision-making systems.
Corresponding efforts will be needed to avoid mischief in  the application of GAI, and to ensure technology does not undercut efforts to enhance  access to justice.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: legal AI should remain assistive, with humans retaining judgment and responsibility, because hallucinations and other reliability limits make verification essential. Its conditional judicial uses and confidentiality safeguards also align with selective, risk-based adoption, though it provides guidance rather than measured evidence on net productivity or verification cost.
qs: Although AI and GenAI can serve as valuable aids in performing certain judicial functions, judges remain solely responsible for their decisions and must maintain proficiency in understanding and appropriately using these tools.
While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report closely supports the cluster’s supervised, task-bounded adoption model: it favors automating routine work while preserving human oversight, treats verification and professional duties as essential, and emphasizes secure tools, training, organizational governance and continuous assessment. Its competence and access-to-justice concerns are largely framed as unresolved risks or conditional forecasts rather than evidence of wholesale lawyer replacement or inevitable deskilling.
qs: AI should augment instead of replace human oversight in legal practice.
While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

st.t: Legal-help evaluation: Resolved problems outrank exam accuracy
st.an: The report supports evaluating AI for real civil legal-help use, protecting users from harmful information, and treating affordability as integral to access to justice. It reinforces implementation through shared evaluated use cases, while offering no evidence that these tools have yet improved legal outcomes and not expressly establishing resolved problems as superior to accuracy metrics.
qs: Rigorous evaluation of AI tools that individuals without lawyers might use for assistance with their civil problems is important to protect the public from inaccurate and potentially harmful information and to facilitate the development of accurate and useful tools.

Otherwise high costs may have the unintended consequence of widening the justice gap by making powerful new legal tools available to clients of means and their lawyers that are not available to low- and moderate-income people and their lawyers.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s principal distinction between useful AI assistance and legitimate judicial authority: judges retain sole responsibility and essential human judgment regardless of AI’s capabilities or efficiency. Its access-to-justice predictions support bounded experimentation, while its warnings about unrebuttable extrajudicial influences reinforce that accuracy alone cannot establish legitimate adjudicative authority.
qs: This foundational principle recognizes that judicial authority is vested solely in judicial officers, not in AI systems.

This includes recognizing that when judicial officers obtain information, analysis, or advice from AI or GenAI tools, they risk relying on extrajudicial information and influences that the parties have not had an opportunity to address or rebut.

st.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI-specific products coexist with heterogeneous, individually tailored coverage and that policy wording is more informative than broad market claims. It adds no malpractice-claims incidence data, so it neither resolves nor challenges the cluster’s central uncertainty.
qs: The insurers offering affirmative AI-specific coverage operate in the surplus lines market, largely free from state insurance commissioners’ regulation of their policy forms, and their terms are typically tailored to fit each individual insured’s specific situation and risks.

Businesses purchasing these novel insurance products should scrutinize their wordings carefully, with the help of counsel if necessary, to make sure that they unambiguously provide the scope of coverage promised and expected.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that legal AI is developing from routine augmentation into strategic operating-model change. It anticipates AI-native firms, lower entry barriers and differentiated competition while emphasizing that secure deployment, human oversight and ethical governance are prerequisites. Its claims are mainly qualitative and predictive, and it offers little direct evidence on bargaining shifts toward legal departments or ALSPs, or on pricing change.
qs: Second, law’s high stakes and the natural caution about injecting AI into it creates an opportunity to create a safety, responsibility, and public interest-first approach to building AI-native law firms and organizations.
AI should augment instead of replace human oversight in legal practice.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core view that AI is currently augmenting lawyers through bounded, low-risk uses rather than enabling autonomous legal delivery. It also supports the cluster’s emphasis on institutional absorption by identifying security, licensing, implementation and specialist-talent costs as constraints that may widen adoption gaps between firms.
qs: In a positive development, lawyers are focused less on whether they will be replaced by generative AI tools and now on how to capitalize on AI tools that will to help them be better lawyers.
Outlook on AI Adoption Early adoption has been limited largely to low-risk, routine tasks where the benefits are clear and the risks are manageable.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The report strongly endorses supervised AI augmentation, continued human accountability, verification, confidentiality safeguards and periodic reassessment. It also directly recognizes—though as an unresolved contributor concern—that verification burdens could reduce or reverse anticipated efficiency gains.
qs: AI should augment instead of replace human oversight in legal practice.

Will we end up with a   briefing process that is less efficient, not more, and thus more expensive, because we will   have to work harder to tell fact from fiction when responding to briefs that were created   using GenAI?

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The report supports human-centered governance, systematic oversight and retained human responsibility for AI-assisted legal and judicial work. It requires human verification, cautions against unreliable or non-authoritative outputs, and treats sanctions as evidence of professional risk, though it provides less detail than the cluster on source-level substantive checking and proportionate verification.
qs: Accordingly, the accuracy of any responses must always be verified by a human.

The tendency of generative AI tools to produce confidently stated but erroneous or false outputs (aka AI “hallucinations”) presents ongoing risks that will require systematic monitoring and oversight.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s central augmentation account: AI is being adopted mainly for routine legal tasks and should complement, rather than replace, human oversight. Its predictions of higher-level work, uneven technological capacity and governance needs align with the cluster’s emphasis on workflow fit and uncertain organisational effects, but provide qualitative claims rather than employment or productivity evidence.
qs: The entry level uses cases – summarizing, extracting insights from unstructured data, drafting simple communications like emails or short memos, and drafting client alerts – still dominate adoption.
AI should augment instead of replace human oversight in legal practice.

kp.k: Legal AI adoption shifts from whether to how
kp.d: The report characterizes the profession’s discussion as moving within one year from resistance and replacement fears toward implementation. Adoption remains concentrated in low-risk, routine uses, while more sophisticated platforms are beginning to connect tasks through robotic process automation or agentic AI.
qs: A year ago, the debate over the use of generative AI focused on ethical concerns for lawyers and protecting the confidentiality of client records.
But as the transformative power of the technology has become more widely known, the conversation has shifted from whether to use the AI technology to how to use it.
The entry level uses cases – summarizing, extracting insights from unstructured data, drafting simple communications like emails or short memos, and drafting client alerts – still dominate adoption.

kp.k: Adoption may divide firms by technological resources
kp.d: The report predicts stratification between firms with and without advanced technology. Professional-grade tools offer more secure environments than consumer products but impose substantial licensing, staffing, training, workflow-development and short-term productivity costs, creating competition for scarce technical expertise.
qs: Predictably, the legal industry is moving toward a stratification of firms into various degrees of technology “haves” and “have-nots.”
While consumer-grade AI tools are becoming increasingly sophisticated, they present privacy and confidentiality risks.
Licensing of professional grade tools is expensive.
The cost of obtaining or training staff to assist the lawyers to exploit fully the capabilities of the tools is higher than expected.
Just as we have seen for decades with new lawyers, there is a developing arms race to obtain, or keep, scarce human resources and expertise.

kp.k: Culture and change management constrain successful implementation
kp.d: The report argues that technical accessibility alone does not ensure effective adoption. Firms must address culture, technophobia, established practices and client-service expectations, accepting additional resources and short-term productivity losses while adapting general tools to specific legal use cases.
qs: Change management appreciating a firm’s unique culture is critical.
Successful adoption requires not only technical training but also proactive strategies to address cultural barriers.
This comes at a cost: adding resources and, in the short term, lost productivity.
It takes time and resources to adapt even the most general tools for a specific use case.
generative AI tools will reduce the cycle time for bespoke tool development, but they will not eliminate it.

kp.k: Firm knowledge systems require costly human curation
kp.d: Firm-wide AI access to accumulated work product exposes obsolete, low-quality or otherwise unsuitable material in document-management systems. The report identifies the creation of exclusion rules and technical controls as unexpectedly difficult and resource-intensive because human oversight remains necessary.
qs: The newfound ability to access the entire body of a firm’s work product and have an AI tool that can incorporate insights from every one of those documents quickly leads to the realization that firm document management systems, like the internet itself, are full of artifacts that the firm would be better off excluding from consideration, whether because of age or quality or obsolescence.
Creating business rules or technological solutions to solve this problem presents more of a challenge than it would seem it should.
Again, this is a resource intensive process as the human oversight required is a major barrier.

kp.k: AI combines automation with higher-level thought partnership
kp.d: The report divides legal-practice use cases into automating repetitive work and augmenting more complex research, analysis and innovation. It predicts that AI will increasingly operate as a thought partner, but recommends combining specialized automation and collaborative uses strategically rather than treating AI output as a substitute for professional judgment.
qs: AI use in law practice generally falls into two main categories.

The first and more established use is leveraging AI to automate repetitive or tedious tasks like organizing emails, freeing up time and resources for legal professionals to focus on more meaningful, high-level work, take on more clients, and overall operate at higher efficiency.

The second, more novel category, is using AI as a creative thought partner to supplement research, casework, and innovation, whether it be delivering personalized education on complex technical topics for legal research or brainstorming interdisciplinary connections across industries for legal advocacy reform.
The optimal integration of AI into legal practice will be both to automate tasks and to collaborate on more complex work.
AI should augment instead of replace human oversight in legal practice.

kp.k: AI may reshape competition and legal entrepreneurship
kp.d: In a contributor reflection, Trooper Sanders argues that law is exposed to strategic disruption because AI can perform high-skill work, lower costs and raise margins. He predicts reduced entry barriers for new practices and firms, including potential benefits for groups with narrower traditional paths to ownership, and advocates safety- and public-interest-first AI-native legal organizations.
qs: But it also means that strategically, law is one of the high-skilled, well compensated guilds in the crosshairs of AI’s disruptive power.
AI’s potential to lower costs and increase margins presents two strategic opportunities.
First, it will reduce barriers to entry enabling legal entrepreneurs and innovators to start practices and grow firms that are better positioned to compete against incumbents.

Second, law’s high stakes and the natural caution about injecting AI into it creates an opportunity to create a safety, responsibility, and public interest-first approach to building AI-native law firms and organizations.

kp.k: AI output can standardize and dilute legal work
kp.d: Matthew Braunel warns that fluent generative AI responses may lack legal or factual grounding and may favor common rather than correct or advocacy-sensitive answers. He speculates that AI could raise the quality floor while lowering the ceiling, and therefore rejects treating current output as final work product.
qs: Another is recognizing the complexities of the output of generative AI platforms which are often articulate and rationale, but are not necessarily based on law or fact.
They may focus on the most common response, rather a correct one, or one that considers elements of advocacy.

There could be a tendency for generative AI output to push work product toward the middle – improving work product that might be considered low quality, but also diluting work product that might be considered high quality.
Based on the current state, generative AI output should not be viewed as the final work product or a replacement for human critical thinking and advocacy.

kp.k: Judges retain responsibility and must verify outputs
kp.d: The judicial working group’s guidelines treat AI as an aid rather than a repository of judicial authority. Judges remain solely responsible for decisions, must guard against automation and confirmation bias, consider disclosure and ex parte concerns, and verify every AI-assisted order, opinion or other work product.
qs: This foundational principle recognizes that judicial authority is vested solely in judicial officers, not in AI systems.

Although AI and GenAI can serve as valuable aids in performing certain judicial functions, judges remain solely responsible for their decisions and must maintain proficiency in understanding and appropriately using these tools.
Users must exercise vigilance to avoid becoming “anchored” to the AI’s response, sometimes called “automation bias,” where humans trust AI responses as correct without validating their results.
Ultimately, judicial officers are responsible for any orders, opinions, or other materials which are produced in their name.
Accordingly, any such work product must always be verified for accuracy when AI or GenAI is used.

kp.k: Courts identify broad but conditional AI use cases
kp.d: The guidelines permit conditional judicial uses including research, document summarization, timelines, editing, authority checking, notices, scheduling, transcription, translation, operational analysis and accessibility. They stress confidentiality controls, reliable training sources and human verification; as of February 2025, no known generative AI tool had eliminated hallucinations.
qs: AI and GenAI tools may be used to conduct legal research, provided that the tool was trained on a comprehensive collection of reputable legal authorities and the user bears in mind that GenAI tools can make errors;
GenAI tools may be used to search and summarize depositions, exhibits, briefs, motions, and pleadings;
AI and Gen AI tools may be used to enhance court accessibility services, including assisting self-represented litigants.
As of February 2025, no known GenAI tools have fully resolved the hallucination problem, i.e., the tendency to generate plausible-sounding but false or inaccurate information.
While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.

kp.k: Dispute resolution gains efficiency but preserves human judgment
kp.d: The report describes current productivity uses for arbitrators, mediators and counsel, including summarization, inconsistency detection, translation, timelines, transcription and mediation coaching. It also reports confidentiality, bias, transparency and enforceability concerns and cites a 2025 study finding materially different negotiating outcomes across AI agents, supporting continued human control over decisions.
qs: Current AI tools can enhance productivity for arbitrators, mediators, and counsel by speeding up traditionally time-consuming tasks, including summarizing lengthy documents, such as deposition or hearing transcripts or expert reports, and providing links to key citations.
AI can even be used as a coach for mediators, providing recommendations and strategies for preparing for mediations and suggesting creative solutions and ways to overcome impasses.
Our findings reveal that AI-mediated deal-making is an inherently imbalanced game -- different agents achieve significantly different outcomes for their users.
Users should exercise caution when delegating business decisions to AI agents.
Human judgment must continue to play a pivotal role in key aspects of dispute resolution proceedings, including decision-making and overseeing the appropriate and responsible use of AI tools.

kp.k: AI could expand access through two pathways
kp.d: The report carries forward two principal access-to-justice mechanisms: increasing legal-services and pro bono lawyer productivity, and directly supplying understandable assistance to people with civil legal problems. These are presented as potential benefits subject to quality improvement, risk mitigation and appropriate human oversight.
qs: The 2024 AI Task Force report detailed the scale of the access to justice crisis in the United States.
It described the potential for generative AI to improve access to justice in two ways:
1.by increasing the efficiency and productivity of legal services and pro bono lawyers, so that they can assist many more people with higher levels of service; and
2.by making accurate, usable, and understandable legal information and assistance easily available to individuals with civil legal problems.

kp.k: Access-to-justice work now includes documented use cases
kp.d: The report identifies progress in training, publicizing use cases, developing quality standards and improving affordability. It cites a Berkeley-related field study and database containing more than 100 legal-aid use cases with ratings, recommendations and estimated efficiency gains, and recommends regular sharing of evaluated applications.
qs: The past year has seen progress on all four high-priority areas identified in the 2024 AI Task Force Report.
“generative AI and Legal Aid: Results from a Field Study and 100 Use Cases to Bridge the Access to Justice Gap,” 57 Loy. L.A. L. Rev. 903 (2024).

The AI Task Force’s website includes a link to a related database that provides detailed descriptions of more than 100 AI use cases for legal aid, including ratings, recommendations, and estimates of efficiency gains resulting from use of the AI tool.
The Task Force recommends regular and widespread sharing of use cases with evaluations like those in Professors Chen’s and Kim’s database.

kp.k: Tool costs could widen rather than close justice gaps
kp.d: The Task Force warns that high subscription prices may deny legal-services providers access to the strongest tools while making them available to wealthier clients and their lawyers. It notes discounted or free initiatives from Thomson Reuters and Everlaw but recommends sustained engagement with developers because current action remains insufficient.
qs: Last year, the AI Task Force cautioned that high subscription costs for the best and most reliable legal AI tools might make those tools unaffordable and inaccessible to the access-to- justice community.
Examples include Thomson Reuters’ AI for Justice Legal Aid Program and Everlaw’s “Everlaw for Good” initiative.
But more needs to be done to expand affordable access.

Otherwise high costs may have the unintended consequence of widening the justice gap by making powerful new legal tools available to clients of means and their lawyers that are not available to low- and moderate-income people and their lawyers.
Financial accessibility to the access-to-justice community must be raised and addressed regularly with legal AI developers.

kp.k: Legal education is integrating AI literacy and practice
kp.d: A 2024 Task Force survey of 29 respondent law schools found that 55% offered AI classes and 83% offered hands-on opportunities such as clinics. The report documents required certification, simulation, legal-aid development and AI-governance coursework, while warning that curricula become obsolete quickly and must preserve ethics and human-centered innovation.
qs: In 2024, the AI Task Force surveyed law school administrators to gain insights on their plans for AI integration into their curricula.
The results showed that 55% of the 29 respondent law schools offered classes on AI, and 83% reported availability of opportunities like clinics where students can learn how to use AI tools hands-on.
All first-year law students are required to take the course, making Case Western the first American law school to require students to earn a certification in legal AI.
“I tell students right up front that half of the substantive material that we cover in this class is probably going to be outdated by the time that you graduate.”

This vigilance, along with upholding professional ethics and prioritizing human-centered innovation, will best prepare law students to successfully navigate how AI will impact the practice of law in the years ahead.

kp.k: Governance must span AI’s full deployment lifecycle
kp.d: The governance discussion argues that conventional compliance is insufficient because AI operates at unusual speed and scale, exhibits expected statistical errors and emergent capabilities, and is governed unevenly across jurisdictions. It recommends frameworks covering strategy, risk management, organizational readiness, policies, operational tools and compliance, with human-centered principles such as transparency, accountability and fairness.
qs: AI governance is essential for managing the unique challenges posed by artificial intelligence, which requires approaches extending beyond traditional compliance frameworks.
Effective governance must address the full lifecycle of AI deployment and its broader implications.
A comprehensive governance framework should encompass six key components: strategy, risk management, organizational readiness, principles and policies, processes and tools, and compliance.
Transparency, accountability, safety, ethics, and fairness are foundational principles that organizations should embed into their AI strategies.
Organizations should adopt a human-centered approach to ensure that AI technologies are used responsibly and effectively, while aligning with evolving legal and regulatory standards.

kp.k: Federal policy prioritizes adoption with high-impact safeguards
kp.d: The report describes the July 2025 White House AI Action Plan as emphasizing deregulation, infrastructure, workforce development and international leadership. Separately, OMB Memorandum M-25-21 requires risk-management practices for high-impact federal AI, including pre-deployment testing, impact assessment, monitoring, staff training and additional human oversight.
qs: America’s AI Action Plan represents a shift in U.S. policy toward AI technology advancement.
As core strategic priorities it emphasizes deregulation, infrastructure expansion, workforce development, and international leadership to ensure American domination of AI technologies.

Agencies are required to follow minimum risk management practices for high-impact AI (defined as “when its output serves as a principal basis for decisions or actions that have a legal, material, binding, or significant effect on rights or safety.”)

The broad range of mandated risk management practices include the conduct of pre-deployment testing and a complete AI impact assessment, ongoing monitoring for  performance and potential adverse impacts, ensuring adequate human trainingand assessment, and providing additional human oversight, intervention, and accountability.

kp.k: Real-world evaluation should complement static benchmarking
kp.d: Schwartz and Waters argue that curated-dataset assessments cannot fully measure practical utility, workforce changes, economic effects or downstream harms. Their proposed real-world evaluation method uses multistakeholder context definition, theories of change, context-informed data, red teaming and field testing to examine how risks and benefits emerge during actual use.
qs: While useful, these computational assessments are too limited to shed light on AI’s secondary and tertiary effects, such as practical utility, workforce and economic shifts, and the downstream impacts of risks in the real world.
Measures of whether specific risks are contained in static output do not provide the higher-order detail necessary to understand AI’s dynamic effects in context.
“Real World AI Evaluation” methods that integrate usage and procedural factors can complement these existing approaches.
The process begins with multistakeholder engagement to specify the evaluation context, produce a theory of change, and systematize the real world phenomena underlying the evaluation’s focus.
Real world testing leverages approaches like red teaming and field testing to collect response data from different types of users as they remotely interact with AI tools.

kp.k: AI complicates allocation of legal liability
kp.d: The report identifies a widening group of potentially responsible actors, including algorithm designers, data collectors, operators and outcome evaluators. Michael Chertoff presents two possible mechanisms—prospective comprehensive regulation or incremental common-law adjudication—without claiming that either alone will resolve allocation questions.
qs: When someone is aggrieved by an AI-driven result, they will seek legal recompense, often through a lawsuit.
Is it the algorithm designer?

The collector and screener of data? The operator who determines the extent of reliance to be placed on AI in decision-making? The evaluator of the outcome with responsibility for corrections and modifications?

One approach is to attempt a comprehensive study of all the facets of an AI driven process, with a view to laying out law and regulations that assign these responsibilities at the outset to those best situated to avoid harms.

The other approach is the traditional common law approach of modifying the law through adjudication of specific fact patterns so that the legal architecture is the sum of individual experiences in varied factual situations.

kp.k: Junior lawyer skill erosion remains an unresolved risk
kp.d: Claudia Ray distinguishes manageable known risks—hallucinations and exposure of confidential information—from uncertain structural consequences. She raises, but does not establish, the possibility that reliance on generative AI could weaken junior associates’ research and drafting formation, increase verification burdens and intensify competition if client industries contract.
qs: The most obvious known pitfalls today include generative AI’s tendency to “hallucinate” and the risk that clients’ confidential information may be exposed if it is uploaded into a generative AI platform.
To me, these known issues are manageable precisely because they are known.
Will reliance on GenAI erode junior associates’ drafting and research skills, resulting in a generation of new lawyers who are simply worse at their jobs?

Will we end up with a briefing process that is less efficient, not more, and thus more expensive, because we will have to work harder to tell fact from fiction when responding to briefs that were created using GenAI?
We don’t know, and that’s what I think we need to be most concerned about.

kp.k: Professional duties apply fully to generative AI use
kp.d: The report summarizes ABA Formal Opinion 512 and numerous state-level opinions and judicial policies. It states that lawyers using generative AI remain bound by competence, confidentiality, communication and reasonable-fee duties, including ensuring that charges reflect the time actually spent when AI changes task duration.
qs: In July 2024 The American Bar Association released Formal Opinion 512 covering the use of generative AI (GAI) in the practice of law.

The ABA opinion states that to ensure clients are protected, lawyers and law firms using GAI must “fully consider their applicable ethical obligations,” which includes duties to provide competent legal representation, to protect client information, to communicate with clients and to charge reasonable fees consistent with time spent using GAI.
Over the past year, many state bar associations and judiciaries have issued ethics opinions and guidance on the use of AI in law practice.
AI ethics opinions outline how lawyers can implement AI in their practices while continuing to meet their professional obligations.

kp.k: AI supports scalable services beyond hourly billing
kp.d: The report’s summary of TECHSHOW 2025 says speakers linked AI-enabled intake and self-help systems to serving latent demand through scalable service models beyond the billable hour. It presents this as an emerging conference theme rather than measured market evidence.
qs: At TECHSHOW 2025 (April 2-5, 2025), 28 of the 72 sessions, or nearly 40%, discussed AI.

Another commonly discussed application was AI’s use in improving client interaction and access to justice via smarter intake systems, chat-based guidance, and tools tailored for self- represented litigants.
Several sessions closely tied the potential of AI to serve the latent legal market to new service models that move beyond the billable hour and increase scalability.
Taken together, these applications reflect a legal field rapidly adapting AI for both operational efficiency and broader system reform.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report describes adoption shifting from whether to use AI toward how to use it, while implementation costs stratify firms.
pts.d: The law-practice authors describe current adoption as concentrated in low-risk summarization, extraction, simple drafting and client alerts, with more sophisticated platforms beginning to chain tasks. They predict technology 'haves' and 'have-nots': secure professional tools require expensive licensing, while implementation also requires scarce technical personnel, training, cultural change and short-term productivity sacrifices. Bespoke development will become faster, not instantaneous. These are qualitative observations and forecasts, not findings from a quantified firm-adoption or cost study (pp. 11–12).

pts.k: The report predicts a combined automation-and-augmentation model, rather than replacement of human oversight.
pts.d: The law-practice authors claim that automation frees legal professionals to undertake higher-level work and serve more clients. They expect AI increasingly to become a creative 'thought partner' for research, argument analysis, risk assessment and interdisciplinary innovation. Effective use can improve productivity, reduce errors and improve client service, but requires appropriate use cases, ethical governance and human oversight. They also describe firm knowledge-management problems: obsolete or low-quality documents must be excluded from AI-accessible work product, requiring resource-intensive human oversight (pp. 12–13).

pts.k: Trooper Sanders predicts lower entry barriers, stronger entrepreneurial competition and opportunities for responsible AI-native practices.
pts.d: Sanders argues that AI's potential to lower costs and increase margins will help new practices compete against incumbents, particularly benefiting women, people of color and others with narrower traditional entrepreneurial pathways. He presents safety- and public-interest-oriented AI-native firms as a strategic opportunity that could also advance U.S. competitiveness if executed well. These are attributed strategic predictions, with no cost estimates or market-outcome data. The separate prediction that AI will upend expert domains is explicitly attributed in Sanders's contribution to venture capitalist Ethan Batraski, whom he quotes (p. 14).

pts.k: Matthew Braunel and Claudia Ray identify possible quality compression, skill erosion and verification-related inefficiency, without asserting these as established outcomes.
pts.d: Braunel suggests that plausible but legally or factually unsupported output could pull work product toward average quality, improving weak work while diluting strong work. He says AI should not replace critical thinking or advocacy in its current state. Ray raises unresolved possibilities: reliance on AI might erode junior associates' drafting and research skills; distinguishing fact from fiction in AI-generated briefs might increase litigation costs; and AI disruption of clients' sectors might reduce demand and intensify competition for legal business. Ray explicitly frames these as questions and unknown risks, not demonstrated effects (pp. 14, 42).

pts.k: The judicial-guidelines authors describe useful court applications but insist that decision-making and output verification remain human responsibilities.
pts.d: Herbert Dixon, Maura Grossman, Allison Goddard, Xavier Rodriguez, Scott Schlegel and Samuel Thumma identify potential uses including research, administrative drafting, document summaries, timelines, editing, scheduling, operational analysis and accessibility. Their guidelines warn that AI-derived information may introduce extrajudicial influences that parties cannot rebut, and that automation and confirmation biases can undermine judgment. They state that no known generative tools had fully resolved hallucinations as of February 2025. These are expert consensus guidelines, not measured productivity results, and are explicitly not presented as the views of the ABA or the entire Task Force (pp. 15–19).

pts.k: Schlegel, Grossman and Dixon anticipate more ethical frameworks and oversight requirements; the report also identifies deepfakes as a growing evidentiary problem.
pts.d: The three contributors predict state and federal efforts over the next two years to address AI in legal and judicial practice. Possible measures include informed consent, transparency about AI's role, supervision of generated outputs and confidentiality safeguards; these are possibilities rather than descriptions of uniformly applicable existing rules. Separately, the report says fabricated media and claims that genuine evidence is fabricated create authenticity, validity and reliability challenges for courts. It links AI-amplified disinformation to declining trust in judicial institutions, drawing on Chief Justice Roberts's 2024 year-end report and security-agency materials (pp. 10, 20, 39–40).

pts.k: The dispute-resolution authors describe productivity benefits while warning against autonomous delegation; Bridget McCormack offers a more expansive market-transformation forecast.
pts.d: The main discussion identifies present capabilities in summarization, comparisons, translation, timelines, transcription and mediation coaching. It qualifies automation with confidentiality, training-data limitations, accuracy, bias, transparency and possible award-enforceability concerns. It cites a consumer-market AI-agent negotiation study reporting unequal outcomes and financial losses; that is cross-domain evidence, not a legal-arbitration trial. McCormack separately says online platforms already use language models for intake, negotiation guidance, evidence analysis, outcome forecasting and award drafting. She predicts accessible, low-cost dispute resolution, profitable micro-claim and cross-border consumer markets, and a shift from rote review to strategic counseling. Her claims about fairness and symmetrical advocacy are not supported here by quantified legal outcome comparisons (pp. 21–23).

pts.k: The access-to-justice authors identify two routes to expanded assistance, while warning that unequal affordability could widen the justice gap.
pts.d: The report argues that AI can increase legal-aid and pro bono lawyers' capacity and provide understandable information and assistance directly to people with civil legal problems. It cites Chien and Kim's 2024 legal-aid field study and a related database of more than 100 use cases with ratings, recommendations and estimated efficiency gains, but does not reproduce numerical gain estimates. It documents vendor discounts and free-access programs, including Thomson Reuters and Everlaw, while warning these are insufficient. Public-facing tools need rigorous quality assessment and continuing improvement; adoption of assessment standards by developers remains an unresolved implementation issue. Samuel Thumma additionally envisions dispute prevention, simpler processes and improved case management, conditional on safeguards against misuse (pp. 24–27).

pts.k: Andrew Perlman predicts that AI adoption will become a competitive and competence imperative within two years.
pts.d: Perlman forecasts increasingly reliable and powerful generative AI, delegation of routine work with oversight, more time for client interactions and advocacy, and affordable legal assistance at scale. He predicts that non-adopters will become less competitive and that professional concern will shift toward the competence of lawyers who do not use AI. These are explicitly forward-looking expert judgments rather than measured findings or an assertion that existing ethics rules already require all lawyers to adopt generative AI (p. 24).

pts.k: The report describes legal education changing toward practical AI literacy, simulation, tool building and governance skills.
pts.d: The authors cite a 2024 survey of 29 responding law schools: 55% offered AI classes and 83% offered opportunities such as clinics for hands-on learning. They characterize this as a national trend, though the figures describe respondents rather than an established population-wide adoption rate. Examples include Case Western's required first-year AI certification program, Suffolk's educational bots and dispute-resolution clinic, Vanderbilt's legal-aid tools, Stanford's negotiation simulator, and NCCU's AI-governance certification preparation. These show curricular initiatives, not measured improvements in graduate competence. Mark Williams separately predicts rapid curricular obsolescence (pp. 28–29).

pts.k: AI creates expanding legal work in governance, liability allocation, transactions, intellectual property and insurance.
pts.d: The Chertoff–Vogel discussion anticipates new liability questions and increased litigation, using autonomous vehicles and medical devices as examples, while emphasizing that discrimination, privacy and copyright laws already apply. Chertoff's separate reflection predicts disputes among designers, data providers, operators and evaluators over responsibility for AI harms, and suggests incremental common-law development may be important. The report describes lawyers as central to AI investments, acquisitions and contracts. Its IP discussion predicts that copyright-training litigation and ownership decisions will shape AI business models and governance. John Buchanan reports emerging AI exclusions and affirmative insurance products, creating a need for careful coverage review. Evidence includes legal authorities, identified insurance products and expert analysis, not quantified forecasts of legal-services demand (pp. 32–45).

pts.k: Reva Schwartz and Gabriella Waters argue that verification burdens and real deployment conditions must be assessed before practical AI value can be established.
pts.d: Schwartz and Waters identify fabricated-citation sanctions as evidence of professional liability risk. They question whether generated briefs create utility when lawyers must check every factual statement. They argue that curated-dataset computational assessments alone cannot establish practical utility, workforce effects or downstream harms, and recommend contextual, multistakeholder evaluation with field testing and red teaming. They cite their 2025 research on an evaluation methodology; the report does not supply an empirical estimate of net legal productivity. Human verification of output and evaluation of deployment effects are distinct activities in this argument (pp. 37–38).

pts.k: The report identifies unequal exposure to automated harms and connects scalable services to possible alternatives to hourly billing.
pts.d: The Civil Rights and Social Justice project reports a 2023 survey of more than 180 attorneys concerning low-income and marginalized clients. Respondents identified opaque automated denials, bias and technology-access problems while reporting limited understanding and confidence. These are attorney-reported perceptions and experiences, not a direct causal audit of the systems. Separately, the TECHSHOW summary says sessions connected AI-enabled service to the latent legal market with scalable models beyond the billable hour; this is a conference-theme account, not evidence of actual pricing-model conversion (pp. 50–51).

pts.k: Individual contributors forecast broader AI developments with consequences for legal governance and human control.
pts.d: Paul Rosenzweig predicts that seconds-scale cyber conflict will require AI responses within human-set boundaries, reducing detailed human-in-the-loop control. He expects semi-autonomous military systems and eventual conflict with accepted conduct limits; these are national-security predictions, not findings about legal-service automation. Stephen Wu predicts eventual AI capabilities exceeding humans and argues that lawyers must prepare governance and rule-of-law safeguards now, without specifying an arrival date. Eric Hibbard reports more than 50 international AI standards and predicts organizational certification opportunities associated with forthcoming ISO/IEC 42006. These claims rest on contributor judgment and, for standardization, identified standards rather than legal-market benchmarks (pp. 42–46).

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines expert forecasts, qualitative practice accounts, limited surveys, named deployments, legal authorities and cited research; it does not provide a unified quantitative test of its transformation claims.
pts.d: The main numerical evidence is the 29-school 2024 survey and the 2023 survey of more than 180 attorneys. Legal-aid evidence includes Chien and Kim's field study and a database with more than 100 use cases, though effect sizes are not reproduced. The consumer-agent negotiation preprint supports a caution about delegated bargaining in its own domain, not a measured legal-dispute outcome. Judicial recommendations rely on the named authors' consensus; the verification discussion cites sanctions incidents, not measured hallucination rates. Governance, IP and insurance discussions identify authorities and market examples. Entrepreneurship, competitive necessity, fairness improvements, future skill erosion and human-level AI are chiefly expert predictions or explicitly unresolved possibilities. The report's disclaimer requires distinguishing its authors' views from an approved ABA institutional position.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report mixes 2023–2025 observations, near-term two-year forecasts and open-ended long-term scenarios.
pts.d: The document is dated December 2025, but its observations and embedded materials have different dates: judicial hallucination guidance is expressly current as of February 2025; the law-school survey is from 2024; the economic-justice survey is from 2023. Reflection boxes answer a question about the next two years and should be understood as near-term expectations rather than assigned more precise end dates. Current law-practice benefits are conditional on suitable tasks, reliable information, security, training, human oversight and change management. Access-to-justice gains require affordable tools and adopted quality standards. McCormack's inclusive dispute-resolution forecast is conditional on responsible implementation. Ray's adverse scenarios remain unanswered questions. Wu's prediction is long-term and indefinite. Neither the report nor its principal forecasts establish a fixed date for wholesale lawyer replacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects are distributed unevenly across providers, entrants, courts, students, corporate buyers and underserved people.
pts.d: Established firms face licensing costs, scarce implementation talent and competition from technologically capable entrants; entrepreneurs from historically constrained groups may gain new pathways. Lawyers may shift from repetitive tasks to strategy, while junior associates face a conjectured skill-development risk. Technical support personnel become more sought after. Judges, clerks, arbitrators, mediators and counsel gain workflow assistance but retain verification and decision responsibilities. Law students and educators encounter new curricula and simulations. Legal-aid and pro bono providers may increase capacity; low- and moderate-income people, self-represented and remote users may obtain assistance or suffer greater inequality if tools are unaffordable or unreliable. Corporate clients require governance, transaction, liability and insurance advice, while AI disruption could also shrink some client sectors. Marginalized communities face particular risks from opaque and biased automated decisions. The report frames enterprise efficiency and unmet civil legal need as related but distinct outcomes.
